info: Direct object — Korean does not have a separate set of direct-object pronouns corresponding exactly to English me, you, him, her, it, and them. Korean uses pronouns such as 나, 너, 그, 그녀, 그것, 그들 and marks the direct object with the particle 을/를: 개가 나를 쫓아요 = “The dog is chasing me.” The pronoun itself generally does not change form because it is the object; the particle shows its grammatical role. Korean also frequently omits object pronouns when they are understood from context, so explicit forms such as 그것을 (“it”) can sound more repetitive than English.
native_answer: the dog is chasing the boy - the dog is chasing him
answer: 개가 소년을 쫓아가. - 개가 그를 쫓아가.

info: Direct – with preposition — Korean does not use prepositions in the same way English does. Instead, particles and postpositional constructions follow the noun or pronoun. For example, with me is 나와, to me can be 나에게, and about me is 나에 대해. The pronoun generally stays the same while the following particle or construction changes. This means that English distinctions such as me in with me, to me, and about me are represented in Korean mainly by 와/과, 에게, 에 대해, rather than by different forms of the pronoun.
native_answer: he is looking at the building - he is looking at it
answer: 그는 건물을 바라봐. - 그는 그것을 바라봐.

info: Indirect — Korean generally marks the recipient or target of an action with 에게, 한테, or 께 depending on context and politeness. For example, 그가 나에게 책을 줘요 = “He gives me the book.” The same 나 can be a direct object when followed by 를: 그가 나를 봐요 = “He sees me.” Thus, the grammatical distinction is primarily expressed by the particle: 를/을 for a direct object and 에게/한테 for a recipient. Korean can also omit the recipient when it is obvious from context.

answer: 나는 식물에 물을 줘. - 나는 그것에 물을 줘.

info: Possessive — Korean expresses possession primarily with 의, although this is frequently omitted or pronounced differently in everyday speech. For example, 나의 책 / 내 책 = “my book,” 그의 기타 = “his guitar,” and 그녀의 바이올린 = “her violin.” The possessor comes before 의 and then the possessed noun. Unlike English, the possessive does not change according to the gender or number of the thing possessed. For standalone possessives such as mine, hers, and theirs, Korean commonly uses 것: 이것은 내 것이에요 = “This is mine,” 이것은 그녀의 것이에요 = “This is hers.” As with other pronouns, Korean frequently leaves the possessor unstated when it is clear from context.
native_answer: I - I am decorating my cake
answer: 나 - 나는 내 케이크를 꾸미고 있어.
